title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.
why: KLS asks whether covariance normalization alone controls the relation between global variation and local change for every log-concave distribution. Its equivalent geometric expansion principle is central to concentration inequalities and the analysis of random walks used for sampling, integration and convex optimization.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in their study of convex-body algorithms, as recounted in the inspected Lee–Vempala survey.
Klartag and Lehec’s Theorem 1.1 bounds reciprocal expansion by \(O((\log n)^5)\).
Klartag’s Theorem 1.2 gives reciprocal expansion \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), equivalent up to constants to a Poincaré bound \(O(\log n)\).
Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell target; the February 2026 revision still distinguishes it from full KLS.
Chen and Klartag’s preprint states the sharp radial variance bound \(8n\), a restricted-observable result rather than full KLS.
Letwin’s preprint states a dimension-free quadratic-form inequality and derives the general Poincaré bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\); this review has not independently verified the new proof.
Zhang’s revised hit-and-run paper explicitly retains KLS as open while reporting progress on a sampling theorem that still depends on its constant.

status_note: The complete all-function KLS conjecture is explicitly open in Letwin’s 27 July 2026 preprint and Zhang’s 5 September 2026 sampling revision. The latter retains dependence on the KLS constant; its claimed mixing theorem does not resolve KLS. Live revision checks and bounded later-work searches on 14 September found no primary full resolution. Thin-shell and quadratic-form results are separately scoped. The new July and September proofs were not independently verified; source statements, conventions and implication directions were checked.

context_blocks.text: Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.

sentences: The KLS conjecture asks for a universal Poincaré inequality for every log-concave probability distribution with zero mean and identity covariance.
Every locally Lipschitz function of finite variance and gradient energy must have its variance bounded by that energy times one constant independent of the dimension and distribution.
The target includes uniform distributions on convex bodies and requires no symmetry, independence or positive curvature assumption.
Its equivalent expansion principle connects high-dimensional geometry and concentration with the analysis of sampling algorithms.
A complete Lean proof must establish the universal bound or its unbounded-counterexample negation; radial, quadratic and dimension-dependent improvements do not settle the full target.
